# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 13 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_013_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 5

**1** After I had written the book as instructed in the earlier vision, the Spirit of God took me up and carried me away to a trackless region. **2** At once the Spirit was changed, and I was able to see the tower clearly; surrounding it were twelve mountains, each with a different appearance. **3** The first mountain was black as soot. The second was bare, with no vegetation. The third was full of thorns and briars. The fourth had herbs growing, half withered at the tops and half green. The fifth had green grass and was quite rugged. The sixth was full of clefts and ravines, some larger and some smaller. The seventh was cheerful and flourishing in every part, with all kinds of animals and birds feeding on it; the more they ate, the more it grew. The eighth was full of springs of water, and every kind of creature the Lord made drank from those springs. **4** The ninth had no water at all and was entirely wilderness, with savage wild beasts and deadly serpents that killed people. The tenth had great trees and was entirely shaded; flocks rested and grazed beneath those trees. The eleventh was densely covered with trees bearing all kinds of fruit; whoever ate desired to eat more. The twelfth was entirely white, and its aspect was radiant and joyful.

---

### Council Notes

The twelve mountains introduce a new spatial-moral scheme to the Vision. They surround the tower (= the Church) and represent twelve categories of people found within the Church. The interpretation is given in later chapters of Vision 3.

The progression from black/soot to entirely white tracks a moral spectrum. The ninth mountain (wilderness, beasts, serpents) is the most dangerous — probably representing apostates who actively harm others. The twelfth (entirely white) represents the fullest expression of holiness.

The seventh mountain (feeding and flourishing) is particularly evocative — a pastoral paradise where grazing produces more growth, not less. This suggests a category of believers whose lives actively generate more life in others.
